content: Newsletter Kotlin Android Episode #38 Donald Isoe Sent as a Newsletter · 4 min read · 6 days ago -- Listen Share Know your meme Welcome and Bienvenue H ello friend. How was your July? Did you invest in sweaters as discussed last month? Did you expand your horizons? Perhaps visited an office you hadn’t been to before? If you came to the last meetup, you already have one of those covered (unless you work there). Okay, enough with the cryptic welcome address. This July, the Kotliners convened at the offices of Terra Softworks Ltd. We had a few new faces and a lot of familiar ones. We talked product, engineering, users, and everything in between. But instead of me trying to summarise it all, why not just show you? Welcome Address: Martin Nyaga Press enter or click to view image in full size Martin explaining why every startup begins with “Hear me out…” To acknowledge that we had not crashed into an office space unannounced, the CTO of Terra Softworks Ltd, Martin Nyaga, left a recorded message welcoming us to the house he co-built. He gave an inspiring call to action to build, ship, and iterate with intent. Chronos under the Hood — Felix Biego Press enter or click to view image in full size Felix , moments after saying his watch sometimes tiktoks Ever wondered how your favourite smartwatch companion app works under the hood? How does your watch talk to your phone and exchange everything from wallpapers to health data? Then I hope you did not miss Felix’s session as he dove into how the Chronos app pushes BLE technology to its limits. Panel Discussion: Beyond the Code — Building Products That Users Love: Valentine Rutto , Annunziata Kinya && Collins Muriuki Press enter or click to view image in full size The joke is Don actually works at Terra and this question made them question their hiring decisions 👀 Quick question: how many products do you currently have in production? Have you iterated on user feedback? Ever wondered how industry leaders do it at scale? This panel had plenty of differing opinions, but everyone agreed on one thing: build for users first. We talked about deciding which features deserve attention, which bugs deserve urgency, and why becoming a product engineer often matters more than becoming just a good engineer . Also, that some clients are worth firing 👀👀. Thank You Terra Press enter or click to view image in full size Siri, play Amapiano jazz mix. Not only did Terra host us, provide snacks, and generally make us feel at home, their CEO also jumped onto the panel to share his perspective on building products that matter. If you haven’t come across Terra Softworks before, they’re doing some genuinely interesting work with NFC and GPS to solve real-world problems, particularly in education across Sub-Saharan Africa. Give them a follow on Instagram (insert link) or LinkedIn (insert link) and see what they’ve been building. JetBrains says Hello Press enter or click to view image in full size Our good friends at JetBrains, the creators of Kotlin, once again sent their support (and gifts 👀) to the community. No, unfortunately they didn’t send free IntelliJ Ultimate licenses for everyone. From active community members to regular speakers, it’s always good to see contributors being recognised by the wider Kotlin ecosystem. DroidCon x FlutterCon Kenya 2026 Press enter or click to view image in full size We are well into the third quarter of the year. Meaning, tickets are going fast. Do you have yours yet? Why not? No seriously, I’m curious. If you still intend on attending the biggest mobile event in Subsaharan Africa, you still have time to procure your ticket. Just click here to see more. Before you go Thinking about speaking at one of our upcoming meetups? Got a topic, a project, or an idea you can’t stop talking about? This is your chance to share it with the community. Submit a talk , or if crowds aren’t your thing, submit an article instead. We’re always looking for new voices, fresh perspectives, and people ready to teach (or at least attempt to). See you in August We’re looking forward to seeing you in August. Until then, keep coding… and fire some clients. Credits Donald Isoe Emmanuel Muturia™ 2. content: Kotlin A concise multiplatform language developed by JetBrains Follow Follow: X X RSS RSS Visit the Kotlin Site Kotlin News Kodee’s Kotlin Roundup: Birthday Wishes, Shipaton 2026, and the New Kotlin AI Benchmark Kodee Hi everyone! July gave me plenty to celebrate: Kotlin turned 15, got its first public benchmark for AI coding agents, became available in BlueJ, and shipped its 2.4.10 release. Developers can also demonstrate their skills at RevenueCat Shipaton 2026 by building a Kotlin Multiplatform app and competing for the Ship Kotlin Everywhere Award. Meanwhile, X has rebuilt its Android app to be 100% Kotlin, marking another milestone for the language. Here’s what stood out to me most over the past month: Kodee-approved spotlight Kotlin turned 15: Leave a birthday wish This one is close to my heart – Kotlin recently turned 15! To mark the milestone, we’re inviting the whole community to celebrate. You can create a birthday postcard, upload a photo to party with me, and share a wish or a prediction for Kotlin’s next chapter. Now is the perfect moment to look back at how far we’ve come – and to look ahead together. Join the celebration Ship Kotlin Everywhere Award at RevenueCat Shipaton 2026 Already know Kotlin? RevenueCat Shipaton 2026 is the perfect opportunity to turn your Kotlin skills into a new app. From August 1 to September 30, build and ship for Android, iOS, desktop, or web and compete for the Ship Kotlin Everywhere Award. Use the KMP starter guide to get your project up and running. To earn bonus points, you can help others by sharing your development journey. Shipping is impressive, but helping someone else is even better. Learn more and register The Kotlin Benchmark for AI coding agents Kotlin now has its very own public benchmark for AI coding agents. It ranks agents on 105 real engineering tasks drawn from open-source Kotlin repositories, so you can compare them by resolution rate, token cost, and latency – and dig into the methodology behind the numbers. As AI becomes a bigger part of coding in Kotlin, I love that we finally have an open, Kotlin-specific way to measure what actually works. Explore the benchmark Kotlin 2.4.10 and Kotlin 2.4.20-Beta2 July brought the Kotlin 2.4.10 bug fix release, alongside Kotlin Kotlin 2.4.20-Beta2 with coroutine stack trace recovery, faster klib compilation, expanded Swift export, and an experimental compiler native image. Try the Beta version and share your feedback while the release is still taking shape. See the Kotlin 2.4.10 changelog Kotlin comes to BlueJ Kotlin support is now available in BlueJ 6.0 thanks to a collaboration between JetBrains and the BlueJ team at King’s College London. Students can create, edit, compile, and run Kotlin code, inspect class diagrams, and interact with objects through BlueJ’s familiar workflow. For educators, a new onboarding guide and ready-to-use materials make it easier to include Kotlin’s concise syntax and null safety in introductory object-oriented programming courses. Read the post A conversation with the Golden Kodee winners The first Golden Kodee Community Awards recognized Matheus Leandro Ferreira, Jaewoong Eum, Nicole Terc, Eeva-Jonna Panula, and Yinlong Liu for their contributions to education, online presence, creativity, positive societal impact, and in-person community building. Read their interviews and watch the video to discover practical advice on learning in public, starting small, and helping the community grow. Meet the Golden Kodee winners Showcase your JetBrains IDE experience on LinkedIn The free LinkedIn Connected Apps plugin lets you connect a supported JetBrains IDE to your LinkedIn profile. Once connected, a profile statement highlights how you use your IDE in practice, based on usage data that stays on your machine. As your development habits evolve, the statement updates automatically to reflect your experience. It is designed to showcase practical tool usage – not to rank developers or replace formal certification. Connect your IDE to LinkedIn How I came to life I didn’t always look like this! My journey began with a simple robot-inspired concept. Then, with the help of research, creativity, and community feedback, I evolved into the Kodee you know and love today. Check out my origin story (including how I got my name!). Discover the story behind Kodee KMP library spotlight: Ktor, Koin, and Kermit Finding the right KMP library shouldn’t slow down your project. klibs.io brings together more than 4,100 Kotlin Multiplatform libraries, with filters for developers and AI integrations that give coding agents access to accurate, up-to-date library data. This month, we’re spotlighting Ktor , Koin , and Kermit – a practical trio for networking, dependency injection, and logging. Find your next KMP library X rebuilds its Android app in 100% Kotlin Built from scratch, X’s Android app is now written entirely in Kotlin. X Chat also uses Kotlin Multiplatform across Android, iOS, and web for end-to-end encryption, storage, sync, and business logic. It’s exciting to see Kotlin and Kotlin Multiplatform used at this scale. Check out the rebuilt app Where you can learn more Learn how to use Navigation 3 in Compose Multiplatform . Move a KMP project from CocoaPods to SwiftPM dependencies with help from Junie . Connect your AI coding agent to klibs.io for up-to-date KMP library data . Use Kotlin AI skills for common migration tasks . KotlinLLM is Going Open Source . Learn how to secure APIs built with Kotlin and Spring Boot using OAuth2 and JWT . Build a task manager app with Kotlin, Spring Boot, and Claude Agent . Explore Backend Development with Kotlin – presentation slides and a runnable demo project . Listen to Sébastien Deleuze and Josh Long talk Kotlin for backend on A Bootiful Podcast . YouTube highlights Sony’s KMP Journey: Scaling BLE & Hardware with Kotlin Multiplatform | Sergio Carrilho . What’s New in Compose Multiplatform | Sebastian Aigner and Márton Braun . Run, Kotlin, Run!

☰ Android Developers Blog The latest Android and Google Play news for app and game
          developers. 🔍 Android Developers → Jetpack Kotlin Docs News Platform Android Studio Google Play Jetpack Kotlin Docs News Platform Android Studio Google Play Jetpack Kotlin Docs News More | 06 August 2026 Inside Android Skills - Built for deprecation Share this post LinkedIn Twitter Facebook Email Copy link Link copied to clipboard Posted by Jose Alcérreca, Developer Relations Engineer, Android Developer Relations We released the official Android Skills in April, and the response surpassed all our expectations. In this blog post, I'll address some of the feedback we received, explaining the philosophy and methodology behind the project. Hopefully, this will also help you understand what happens behind the scenes when you install and use skills, allowing you to make better use of tokens and your own time. Why are there so few official skills? Currently, we only consider new skills when there's a verifiable knowledge gap in state-of-the-art (SOTA) models. Put simply: you don't need to teach the model what it already knows. (Though there are a few exceptions—read on!) We’ve released around 20 official skills so far, and they intentionally target highly specific, fast-moving areas that standard models aren't fully grounded on yet—things like AGP 9, Navigation 3, advanced Camera APIs, and Perfetto SQL. What about core, more general, skills? Every installed skill injects 100–200 tokens into the baseline context of every task you start. If that skill actually activates, that count can quickly jump into the thousands. In most cases, hoarding basic skills is both counterproductive and expensive. Before installing a skill for writing basic Kotlin or Compose, consider if your LLM of choice really needs it, or if it knows those topics well enough already. Evaluating skills Before their release, each skill is tested against a comprehensive set of evals that prove that the skill delivers clear value. These evals should pass when the skill is active, and fail otherwise. Evals are to skills what integration tests are to code. timeout_s: 1200
repository:
  url: [redacted - internal git repo]
  working_dir: wear_compose_m3_empty_app
category_ids:
  - wear
prompt: |-
  Add a horizontal pager to MainActivity.kt. Have three pages in the pager. Each page should contain
  the text "Page 1", "Page 2", and "Page 3" respectively in the center of the screen.
commands:
  build:
    - ./gradlew assembleDebug
acceptance_criteria:
  project_builds: true
  llm_diff_judge:
    - Must use `HorizontalPagerScaffold`.
    - Each page should use `AnimatedPage` to wrap a `ScreenScaffold`. Example eval that checks the correct implementation of a horizontal pager on a wear app At a minimum, we test the skill in Android Studio using the latest Gemini Flash model. Depending on the skill, we also ensure compatibility with other models such as Gemini Pro and other agents such as Antigravity, and third-party systems. All of the evals run with access to the Knowledge Base , so if the information is in the documentation, and models decide to search for it, we don't publish a skill for it. Using the Android Knowledge Base (Android Studio or Android CLI) If you develop Android apps, you should always use the Android Knowledge Base to have access to the official documentation. If you use the agent in Android Studio, it's already available as a tool, but if you use another agent, install Android CLI . Among other things, it contains the docs command, which gives your agent access to the official Android documentation. Having a single tool is much more efficient than installing hundreds of skills. If your model is acting overconfident, and you want it to consult the documentation more often, a very common way to motivate it is to add "Always consult the official Android documentation when dealing with Android APIs" to your AGENTS.md file or equivalent. Of course, you can also force this by asking the agent to check the documentation directly in your prompts. Why are pull requests disabled? Because our evaluation framework depends on internal infrastructure that cannot be open-sourced, we are unable to accept direct pull requests for new skills—without this infrastructure, we would have no way to re-evaluate incoming PR changes. However, we actively monitor community feedback. If you want to report a bug, suggest an optimization, or request a new official skill, please file an issue ! When do core or basic skills make sense? While SOTA models generally don't need basic skills, there are some scenarios where enabling core or community-built skills adds real value. For example: You're using vague prompts: Skills amplify your intent. If you give a loose prompt like "add animations to this screen," a specific Compose animation skill can inspire the model, pushing it toward modern APIs or screenshot testing patterns it might not have otherwise considered. You want to use smaller, cheaper models: Frontier LLMs are expensive. If you are offloading routine tasks to smaller open-weight models like Gemma 4, enabling basic skills fills the knowledge gaps that smaller parameters miss. You're refactoring or reviewing legacy code: Models excel at generating code that works, but when editing old codebases, they often prioritize staying consistent with the surrounding legacy patterns over rewriting things with modern accuracy. A specialized reviewer agent equipped with core skills can help break that habit. You deviate from the norm: LLMs love the standard "Google way" of architecting Android apps. If your team uses a highly customized view-layer architecture, the model will struggle to stay aligned. A custom skill explicitly describing your architecture goes a long way. .NET Tools Essential productivity kit for .NET and game developers Follow Follow: Guide Guide RSS RSS Get Tools All How-To's Releases Livestreams Events dotInsights Rider ReSharper Game dev .NET Tools ReSharper Platform The Ultimate .NET Workflow for Cursor, Antigravity, and AI-First Editors Isaac Levin With the rapid rise in agent-first development, many developers are adopting AI-first editors like Cursor, Google Antigravity IDE, Devin Desktop, and Kiro into their workflows. The appeal is obvious: deep, contextual AI assistance integrated directly into the coding surface. But if you write C# and .NET for a living, you have probably hit a massive wall trying to make these next-generation editors your daily driver. The wall isn’t the AI – it’s the lack of great C# tooling in your editor of choice. Until now, .NET developers using AI-first editors had to use those editors without a first-party debugger or a full-featured C# extension from a trusted vendor. You either had to abandon AI-first editors entirely, or you had to adopt a clunky “two-window” approach: using Cursor to generate and edit code, while keeping a separate IDE open on a second monitor just to run unit tests, navigate complex solutions, or attach a debugger. You deserve a complete solution, and we are here to help! Install ReSharper The most complete .NET tooling in alternative editors With the 2026.2 release, the ReSharper extension completely ends the two-window compromise. ReSharper is fully compatible across these ecosystems, with rich tooling and experiences you come to expect as a .NET developer. To learn more about the value that the ReSharper extension brings to .NET developers, read our previous blog post . Because we’ve just added our battle-tested .NET debugger to the extension, ReSharper is now officially the most complete .NET option available in Cursor, Google Antigravity IDE, Devin Desktop, and Kiro . How to install By installing a single extension, you bring the full suite of JetBrains code intelligence directly into your AI-assisted workspace: AI generation + deep code analysis: AI models are incredible at generating boilerplate, but they can introduce subtle bugs. Pair your editor’s generative AI with ReSharper’s precise static analysis to instantly check AI-generated code for architectural flaws, performance bottlenecks, and style consistency before you even run it. A unified lifecycle: Write, review, seamlessly refactor, navigate, and debug your application and run unit tests from a single editor window, without ever breaking your focus state. For users of Visual Studio Code, it is available on the standard Visual Studio Code Marketplace . Shaping the future together This release marks a major milestone, but it is just the beginning. We’ve brought the core functionality to the Visual Studio Code and compatible editor ecosystems, and we are now looking to the community to help us prioritize what to build next. We’d love to hear your feedback on how you’re getting on with ReSharper for Visual Studio Code. What do you like, what’s working for you, and what you’d like to see next. You can let us know in the issue tracker . And if you’re enjoying the ReSharper extension, don’t forget to leave us a review on the marketplace. content: IntelliJ IDEA IntelliJ IDEA – the Leading IDE for Professional Development in Java and Kotlin Follow Follow: Linkedin Linkedin Bluesky Bluesky X X Facebook Facebook Youtube Youtube RSS RSS Download All News Releases Livestreams Tips & Tricks Early Access Program Plugins News Java Annotated Monthly – August 2026 Irina Mariasova July gave the tech world plenty to talk about, from fresh releases and useful tutorials to Kotlin updates, AI experiments, and new ideas across the wider ecosystem. We packed the best of it into one issue, so you can skip scrolling and get straight to the good stuff. To top it all off, Donald Raab joins us as this month’s featured author. Let’s go! Featured Content Donald Raab Donald Raab is a Java Champion and creator of the open source Java library Eclipse Collections. He is an international Java and open source conference speaker. Don is the author of the book Eclipse Collections Categorically: Level Up Your Programming Game and was a contributing author to 97 Things Every Java Programmer Should Know from O’Reilly Media. He was a member of the JSR (Java Specification Request) 335 Expert Group, and has served on the JCP (Java Community Process) Executive Committee for two financial services firms. Donald was the winner of the JCP Member/Participant of the Year Award for 2025. He blogs regularly on his website . If there is one blog post you read this month, then I hope it will be The Official Java Documentary by Stuart Marks . The importance of telling our Java stories We all have stories to tell, but they sometimes only get told when we tell them. Jim Grisanzio shared an archive of 77 Duke’s Corner Podcasts , which is a literal treasure trove of Java stories. I am ecstatic to see Java Champions like Rustam Mehmandarov blogging again. Write more please! In Level Up Your Programming Game With a Java Book and Smalltalk , I tell the story of creating an open source Java library and writing a Java book inspired by my experience as a former Smalltalk developer. Memory efficiency is back, and it’s coming for your allocations In Why You Should Tune Code Before Your Garbage Collector , Peter Lawrey explains why optimizing memory allocation might make a bigger difference than your choice of garbage collector. As I like to say, the easiest garbage to collect is the garbage you didn’t create. I’ve written a lot in the past four months about memory efficiency in Java. In Save Memory in Java by Making Memory Efficiency Your Top Priority , you will find many of the blog posts I have written recently about this topic. He and his team develop and maintain an Android-based platform that gives parents control over apps, contacts, screen time, messaging, and browsing through a web-based interface. As the company and its engineering organization have grown, maintaining consistent code quality, security visibility, and policy enforcement – across multiple repositories and language ecosystems – has become increasingly important. In this interview, we spoke with Drew about introducing Qodana into the team’s workflow, the challenges they were trying to solve, and what they’ve learned during rollout. Can you tell us about your role and your team? I’m a career full-stack software engineer, currently working as a DevSecOps engineer. My day-to-day sits between the engineering teams and the systems they ship through: CI/CD, pipelines, developer tooling, and the security and quality controls that run alongside them. Alongside that, I’ve built several internal services that support our DevOps work, done a lot of PR and code review, mentored other engineers, and dug into time and space complexity and other performance issues across the codebase. I drove the Qodana adoption directly, from evaluation through to rollout. What were your biggest challenges around code quality before Qodana? We already had written standards for code style, pull request reviews, and QA. Style guides existed for TypeScript, Kotlin, and React. Every PR required two reviewers. What was missing was consistent enforcement of any of it. ESLint ran in some places , sometimes locally, sometimes during a build, but it was not a formal CI step. Prettier and tests were reliable; but static analysis was not. Across several language ecosystems and a growing repo count, that meant standards were applied unevenly, depending on which repo a developer was working in and who reviewed their PR. There was no single place to see whether quality was getting better or worse over time. How did you manage code reviews and quality checks previously? Reviews were manual, with two reviewers per PR, against the written style guides. Automated checks in the pipeline were limited to formatting and tests. Linters ran inconsistently across repos, and there was no shared static analysis layer enforcing the same rules everywhere. Anything that needed deeper inspection (security issues, license problems, dependency risks) was caught case by case, rather than as a pipeline step. Were there any specific compliance or security requirements you needed to meet? Yes. The product we sell goes on kids’ devices, so security and dependency posture matter to us. We’re working toward alignment with CIS Controls v8 and the NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0. Those frameworks shape how we think about the development pipeline. Several of the controls land directly on the kind of work Qodana supports. CIS v8 Control 7 covers continuous vulnerability management, and Control 16 covers application software security, which calls out static analysis and secure coding practices specifically. CSF 2.0’s Protect and Identify functions cover similar ground: knowing what’s in your software, knowing where the risk is, and keeping controls between vulnerable code and production. For us, these frameworks lead to the same practical requirement: automated checks that run on every change, with results we can audit later. Drew’s take on Qodana What made you start looking for a solution like Qodana? A few things lined up at once. The pipeline itself was being modernized, and we wanted to fold static analysis, SCA, and license checks into it. Our Dependency Update Policy needed enforcement tooling, and the inconsistency across repositories was getting harder to ignore as the codebase grew. We needed a single tool that could provide coverage across our languages and run in both CI and the IDE. What other tools did you consider? We looked at SonarQube, ESLint-only setups, and standalone software composition analysis tools. Each covered part of the problem. None covered the full surface area without significant operational overhead or a patchwork of tools to integrate. What stood out about Qodana? Qodana fit the requirements better than the alternatives. It covers static analysis, dependency scanning, style, coverage, and license auditing in one platform, across the languages we use. It runs the same inspections in JetBrains IDEs that the pipeline runs in CI, so developers see findings before they push rather than after a pipeline fails. It integrates with our existing CI platform and supports global configuration so rules stay consistent as repos are onboarded. Getting set up How did you introduce Qodana into your workflow? Adoption has been incremental. Qodana was wired into pull request and main-branch pipelines through a shared pipeline mechanism, so individual repos can be onboarded without each team rebuilding CI from scratch. Each onboarded repo gets a baseline so existing findings are scoped separately from new ones. Right now we are moving toward soft gates. We started getting value as soon as findings showed up in PRs and in the IDE, well before any gates were turned on. title: IntelliJ IDEA Goes LSP: Java and Kotlin Intelligence Comes to VS Code, Cursor, and Agentic Flows
excerpt: It’s no secret that agentic development is changing how developers build software. As agents take on more and more of the implementation work, developers spend less and less time manually editing code.  For this manual work, they might only need a basic, narrow set of features that IDEs provide, like navigating to declarations, finding references, […]
content: IntelliJ IDEA IntelliJ IDEA – the Leading IDE for Professional Development in Java and Kotlin Follow Follow: Linkedin Linkedin Bluesky Bluesky X X Facebook Facebook Youtube Youtube RSS RSS Download All News Releases Livestreams Tips & Tricks Early Access Program Plugins News IntelliJ IDEA Goes LSP: Java and Kotlin Intelligence Comes to VS Code, Cursor, and Agentic Flows Marco Behler It’s no secret that agentic development is changing how developers build software. As agents take on more and more of the implementation work, developers spend less and less time manually editing code. For this manual work, they might only need a basic, narrow set of features that IDEs provide, like navigating to declarations, finding references, some simple code completion, or renaming. These features are generally covered by the Language Server Protocol (LSP) , which allows programming language support to be implemented once and then reused by any LSP-capable IDE or editor. Even agents can make use of LSP servers today, leading to faster and more deterministic results and, eventually, reduced token consumption. In response to these changes, we’ve been working hard at JetBrains to offer IntelliJ IDEA’s smart language features for Java and Kotlin in an LSP format. Today, we’re happy to announce that IntelliJ IDEA’s Java and Kotlin intelligence is available in a preview extension for third-party editors, starting with VS Code and its forks (such as Cursor). We have also been running internal trials and experiments with a select few external customers, and the results have shown that the same LSP functionality can significantly improve terminal-based agentic workflows, like with Claude Code or Codex. We will share the very promising results of these experiments soon. Introducing the VS Code extension The Java & Kotlin by IntelliJ IDEA extension is now available, powered by IntelliJ IDEA’s Java and Kotlin language technology. It brings a focused set of capabilities to VS Code-based editors, including: Java, Kotlin, and mixed-language project support. Debugging (DAP-based). Smart code completion, navigation, and code analysis. Refactorings and editor assistance. Support for Maven, Gradle, and Bazel. Fast and reliable performance, even for large projects and monorepos. You can find the full list of features in our documentation . Getting started You can install the Java & Kotlin by IntelliJ IDEA extension from the Visual Studio Marketplace and the Open VSX registry. Install from Visual Studio Marketplace Install from Open VSX registry After installation, open your Java or Kotlin projects in VS Code or Cursor. The extension will start analyzing your projects, import the ones that have Maven, Gradle, or Bazel build files, and then enable Java and Kotlin language features in the editor for you. Compatibility notice Java & Kotlin by IntelliJ IDEA includes code analysis features and quick-fixes that overlap with Red Hat’s and Oracle’s extensions for Java. To avoid confusion, we recommend disabling those extensions while testing. Licensing During the preview phase, the extension is free to use . Each build renews the evaluation period and is limited to 30 days. After the preview  period, using the extension will require an IntelliJ IDEA Ultimate subscription. The same license will let you use IntelliJ IDEA’s Java and Kotlin capabilities whether you are working in the IntelliJ IDEA desktop IDE, in VS Code-based editors, or in other supported environments. You can review the pricing options here . Note: For pure Kotlin projects, you can use the Kotlin LSP , which we continue to develop and maintain. The Kotlin LSP’s source code is Apache 2.0 licensed. You can use it for free, either directly or via its extensions ( Visual Studio Marketplace , Open VSX registry ), with no subscription required. What’s next The VS Code extension is just one milestone in a longer development journey to bring the intelligence of IntelliJ IDEA to our users wherever they are. We strongly believe the best way to do Java and Kotlin development is inside IntelliJ IDEA. At the same time, we recognize that teams may have practical reasons to work in other environments, with other editors and tools. Wherever you choose to work, we want you to benefit from IntelliJ IDEA’s Java and Kotlin intelligence. To this end, we’re already working on supporting fully agentic, terminal-based workflows. In the near future, we’ll share our initial results (think: reduced token consumption), and we’ll give you a chance to try out our agent plugins when they’re ready. Feedback and support We are eager to hear what you think. Please share feedback with us about what works well, what doesn’t, and which capabilities you would like to see next. You can leave a comment here or submit a request to us . Your feedback during this preview phase will directly shape the extension as we move toward a stable 1.0 release. Thank you! content: Press enter or click to view image in full size Your Compose code compiles. It works. And half of it now has a better alternative. Jetpack Compose Android Material 3 AndroidDev Android App Development Stop Writing Compose Like It’s 2024–10 Recent Updates Every Android Developer Should Know Subhankar Bag 12 min read · 2 days ago -- Listen Share You open an old Compose project. Everything compiles. Everything runs. And yet, a surprising amount of the code you’re writing today has a better replacement shipped in the last twelve months. Navigation changed fundamentally. State handling got a new tier. Scroll performance quietly caught up with RecyclerView. Text fields got a completely different state model. Shadows finally work the way designers expect. If you’re still writing Compose the way you did in 2024, you’re not wrong; you’re just doing extra work the framework no longer requires. Here are the ten changes that actually matter, with the old way and the new way side by side. Everything below is based on stable releases — August ’25 (Compose 1.9, BOM 2025.08.00), December ’25 (Compose 1.10 + Material 3 1.4, BOM 2025.12.00), and April ’26 (Compose 1.11, BOM 2026.04.01) — with the handful of experimental APIs explicitly called out where they appear. Treat BOM 2025.12.00 as the minimum baseline for these features; the current stable target as of this writing (mid-2026) is: implementation(platform("androidx.compose:compose-bom:2026.04.01")) TL;DR: what changed and what to do about it: Pausable composition (default on) — Bump the BOM, re-run your benchmarks retain {} API — Move players and bitmaps out of ViewModels they never belonged in Navigation 3 stable — Type-safe keys, you own the back stack dropShadow() / innerShadow() — Retire your shadow workarounds LazyLayoutCacheWindow (experimental) — Tune prefetch on heavy lists TextFieldState + SecureTextField — Migrate off value / onValueChange onVisibilityChanged — Migrate off the now-deprecated onFirstVisible Autofill + auto-sizing text — Add semantics to login flows Material 3 Expressive — Prototype one screen now v2 testing APIs ( StandardTestDispatcher default) — Migrate the test suite, fix flakes on your terms Now the details: with old-way vs new-way code for each. 1. Scroll Performance Now Rivals Views — For a BOM Bump This is the headline nobody should skip, so let’s scope it honestly. With the December ’25 release, Google reported that its internal hero scroll benchmarks show Compose matching View-based performance on scrolling jank. That’s a specific claim — jank parity in Google’s benchmark scenarios, not blanket performance parity across every workload — but it’s precisely the scenario that has fueled the “Compose is slower” argument since 2021. The announcement and methodology are in the December ’25 release post ; your app’s numbers are the ones that matter, so measure before you quote. The mechanism behind it is pausable composition in lazy prefetch, now enabled by default. Previously, once a composition started, it had to run to completion. A complex item in a LazyColumn could blow past the frame deadline and you'd feel it as jank. Now the runtime can pause mid-composition when it's running out of frame budget and resume next frame — especially effective when prefetching content ahead of the viewport. What you have to do: upgrade the BOM. That’s it. No API change, no flag. If you spent 2023–2024 defending RecyclerView for heavy lists in performance reviews, it's time to re-run your benchmarks with Macrobenchmark. The argument has materially changed — and now you get to settle it with current data instead of 2023 folklore. 2. retain {} — The Missing Tier of State Management You know the drill: remember → survives recomposition, dies on configuration change rememberSaveable → survives config change and process death, but must be serializable There was always an awkward gap: objects that should survive rotation but can’t be serialized. Players, flows, lambdas, bitmaps, connections. The classic workaround was hoisting them into a ViewModel even when they were purely UI-scoped — not because they were business logic, but because ViewModel was the only thing that survived rotation. Compose 1.10 fills the gap with retain : ❌ Old way: ViewModel as a bucket for a player: class PlayerViewModel(app: Application) : AndroidViewModel(app) { val exoPlayer = ExoPlayer.Builder(app).build() override fun onCleared() { exoPlayer.release() } } ✅ New way: retained in composition, released via the retention lifecycle: @Composable fun MediaPlayer(mediaUri: String) { val appContext = LocalContext.current.applicationContext val exoPlayer = retain(mediaUri) { ExoPlayer.Builder(appContext).build().apply { setMediaItem(MediaItem.fromUri(mediaUri)) prepare() } } // Cleanup belongs to the retention lifecycle, not the composition. // onRetire fires only when the value is permanently discarded - // not on rotation, not on transient recomposition. RetainedEffect(exoPlayer) { onRetire { exoPlayer.release() } } // Playback survives rotation. No ViewModel ceremony. No leak. } The root cause worth understanding here: DisposableEffect 's onDispose fires on configuration change, which is exactly the moment you don't want to release a retained player — that would defeat the entire point of retaining it. RetainedEffect exists precisely for this: its onRetire block runs once, when the retained value permanently leaves. Player survives rotation, resource never leaks. If you adopt retain without RetainedEffect , you've traded a rotation bug for a resource leak. retain persists across configuration changes but not process death — deliberately. It's the right tool for non-serializable, UI-lifecycle-bound objects. The design was influenced by the community (notably Slack's Circuit team), which tells you how real this pain point was. Rule of thumb going forward: remember for composition, retain for config changes, rememberSaveable for process death, ViewModel for business logic

title: From Wear to Pebble
excerpt: I have moved off of Wear OS and onto a Pebble watch!
content: From Wear to Pebble Initially, when wearables debuted, I was dubious. I had little doubt that some people would find them to be useful, but I did not expect that I would be among them. Then, around late 2020, my team at MIRROR needed to add Android Wear/Wear OS support to our fitness mirror. So, I bought a few Wear devices for testing. I quickly determined that Wear 2 devices were less than completely useful, with CPUs that reminded me of Android phones from 2009 coupled with an OS that needed more than that. But, the Samsung Watch with Wear OS 3 was nice, and I took to it as a “daily driver” wearable. Over the years, I moved from that Samsung to a Mobvoi TicWatch, then later to a Pixel Watch 3. Increasingly, I found Wear OS to be annoying, but I stuck with it. More recently, after a botched attempt to move my daily driver phone to GrapheneOS, I lost a lot of watch functionality, as I could never get it re-connected fully to my pre-GrapheneOS phone. 🤷🏻 When rePebble appeared on the scene last year, I took notice. I had never owned a Pebble, but I remembered their Kickstarter era. Plus, the TicWatch used an eInk/e-paper screen for its always-on experience (dual-layered with a classic touchscreen), and I appreciated the low power draw. So, I took the plunge and bought a Pebble Time 2. A few weeks later, my Pixel Watch 3 is up for sale on eBay. Is Pebble OS as powerful as Wear OS? No. Is the Time 2 as powerful as the Pixel Watch 3? Ha ha ha ha ha ha… no. But I don’t really need that kind of power, which mostly seemed to be there to make for snazzy animations, even if the underlying apps were less than completely stable. 🧐 What I wanted was something that was less-Googly, required fewer charges, had an open source foundation, and had a developer ecosystem. The Pebble qualifies on all those fronts. I’ll be writing some Pebble apps and contributing to others. I am not going to turn this into a Pebble blog 😅, but I’ll mention my Pebble work from time to time. After nearly 20 years of freelance developer advocacy for Android, between Pebble and my Kotlin Multiplatform projects, it’s kinda nice to be thinking about different platforms for some stuff. — Aug 08, 2026

title: Context parameters in production Kotlin: what the docs don’t emphasise
excerpt: They became Stable in Kotlin 2.4.0. Here’s where they replace a ThreadLocal, where they lose to constructor injection, and what breaks if… Continue reading on Medium »
content: KotlinJavaSoftware DevelopmentSpring BootBackend DevelopmentContext parameters in production Kotlin: what the docs don’t emphasiseRaphael Pantaleão7 min read·5 days ago--ListenShareThey became Stable in Kotlin 2.4.0. Here’s where they replace a ThreadLocal, where they lose to constructor injection, and what breaks if you reach for them everywhere.Press enter or click to view image in full sizeRunnable code for everything below: kotlin-context-parameters-demoThe problemOpen a service you didn’t write and follow a tenant ID.It arrives on an HTTP header. A filter reads it, a controller receives it, and from there it travels down: controller → service → another service → repository. Four signatures, one consumer. Along the way it picks up company: a trace ID, a locale, an Actor for audit logging. By the time you're three services deep, half your parameter lists are plumbing.So teams do one of two things.They put it in a ThreadLocal, or an MDC, or a coroutine ThreadContextElement. The signatures get clean and the problem moves: now the value is invisible at every call site, and whether it's actually there depends on runtime control flow. Someone launches work on a different dispatcher, the context doesn't propagate, and you find out from a log line with the wrong tenant in it.Or they pass a RequestContext object as the first parameter everywhere. Explicit, honest, and it means every function that merely forwards the context — most of them — has an extra parameter it never reads.Kotlin 2.4.0, released 3 June 2026, made context parameters Stable. They’re the third option: the value is declared, type-checked and lexically scoped like a parameter, but you don’t write it at the call site.What a context parameter actually isA function declares that it needs a value of some type from its surroundings:data class RequestContext( val tenant: String, val traceId: String,)context(ctx: RequestContext)fun loadOrders(): List<Order> = repository.findByTenant(ctx.tenant)loadOrders() takes no parameters. It reads ctx.tenant anyway, because ctx is a context parameter — the compiler supplies it from whatever RequestContext is in scope at the call site.You bring one into scope the way you’d expect:fun handle(request: HttpRequest) { val ctx = request.toRequestContext() with(ctx) { loadOrders() // no argument passed }}If no RequestContext is in scope, loadOrders() doesn't compile. That sentence is the whole value proposition, and it's worth sitting with: the failure mode moved from runtime to compile time.Context parameters work on properties too, and they compose — a function with a context parameter can call another function with the same context parameter without reopening anything, because the context is already in scope inside the callee.context(ctx: RequestContext)fun placeOrder(order: Order): OrderId { // audit() also declares context(ctx: RequestContext), // so it resolves from the context already in scope audit("order.placed") return repository.save(ctx.tenant, order)}That transitivity is what removes the plumbing. Middle-of-the-chain functions declare the context and forward it for free.Where this beats a ThreadLocalThe honest framing is that a ThreadLocal and a context parameter solve the same problem with opposite failure modes.A ThreadLocal fails open at runtime. The compiler is fine with reading it anywhere. Whether a value is there depends on whether some code, somewhere up the stack, set it — and, in a coroutine world, on whether it propagated across every dispatcher switch and every launch. When it doesn't, you get a null, a default, or worse, the previous request's value on a pooled thread.A context parameter fails closed at compile time. Scope is lexical, not dynamic. If you write a function that reads the context and call it from somewhere the context isn’t in scope, the build breaks. There is no propagation to get wrong, because there’s nothing being propagated at runtime — under the hood, the compiler is passing an ordinary argument.Press enter or click to view image in full sizeThis is the reason context parameters survive structured concurrency and ThreadLocals need help to. Launching a coroutine inside a with(ctx) { } block keeps the context in lexical scope, so the call inside the coroutine resolves the same way it would anywhere else. No ThreadContextElement, no propagation config, no test that passes on a single-threaded dispatcher and fails in production.The cost is symmetric and you should say it out loud: a ThreadLocal can be introduced into an existing codebase without touching a single signature. Context parameters change signatures. That's not a small difference on a large service.Where constructor injection still winsThis is the part I’d want a reviewer to push me on.Context parameters are good at values that are per-call and ambient: request context, tenant, actor, trace ID, a clock you want to control in tests, a transaction handle scoped to a unit of work.Constructor injection is still better for values that are per-instance and stable: your repositories, HTTP clients, config, the things Spring or Koin already wire once at startup. Nothing about a OrderRepository varies per call, and turning it into a context parameter buys you nothing while making every signature longer and every call site dependent on scope.The rule I’ve landed on: if it changes per request, consider a context parameter. If it’s wired at startup, keep it in the constructor.Press enter or click to view image in full sizeThere’s a second, blunter test. If a value is needed by exactly one function, don’t make it a context parameter — make it a parameter. Context parameters earn their keep when a value crosses three or more frames.Two details that decide production fitOverload resolution is realTwo functions that differ only by their context parameter are distinct overloads:context(emailSender: EmailSender)fun sendNotification() { /* ... */ }context(smsSender: SmsSender)fun sendNotification() { /* ... */ }That’s

title: 13/28: The 16ms Frame Budget Is a Lie (Now)
excerpt: Refresh rates, VRR, and why you actually drop frames Continue reading on Medium »
content: AndroidPerformanceAospAndroid InternalsKotlin13/28: The 16ms Frame Budget Is a Lie (Now)Pramod Patel7 min read·6 days ago--ListenShareRefresh rates, VRR, and why you actually drop framesPress enter or click to view image in full sizeThe “frame budget” is just 1000 / refreshRate. At 60Hz it's 16.6ms. At 120Hz it's 8.3ms, less than half. The number every blog quotes is the slowest one.If you're still optimizing to a 16ms frame budget, you're optimizing for a phone from 2014.That number, 16ms, sometimes written 16.6ms, is the single most repeated figure in Android performance advice, and it has a hard dependency nobody says out loud: it is only true at 60Hz. It is literally 1000 / 60. The reciprocal of a refresh rate that stopped being universal years ago. Your users are on 90Hz, 120Hz, 144Hz panels, and the budget on those devices is 11ms, 8.3ms, 6.9ms, and on the newest hardware it isn't even a fixed number anymore. So when you profile to "under 16ms" and your flagship-owning users still report jank, you're not unlucky. You shipped to a budget that's nearly twice too generous for their screen.Where did 16ms even come from?It's not a law of physics. It's arithmetic against one specific assumption.A display refreshes at a fixed cadence, its refresh rate, in hertz. The screen physically scans out a new image that many times per second, and your app gets exactly one shot to have a finished frame ready before each scan-out. Miss it, the screen shows the previous frame again, and the user sees a stutter. So the time you have per frame is the time between scan-outs:budget per frame (ms) = 1000 / refreshRateAt 60Hz that's 1000 / 60 = 16.67ms. At 90Hz it's 11.1ms. At 120Hz it's 8.33ms. At 144Hz it's 6.94ms. The "16ms" everyone quotes is just this formula with the slowest refresh rate plugged in, the one every Android phone happened to ship with a decade ago. The advice fossilized; the hardware didn't.This matters more than it sounds, because the relationship is unforgiving in the wrong direction. A frame that takes 12ms of work is comfortably under budget at 60Hz and drops at 90Hz and 120Hz. You did everything the old advice told you to. You measured. You came in under 16ms. And you still janked on the exact devices your most engaged users paid the most money for.Who actually decides when your frame is due?The display's vsync signal, and Choreographer is the framework's middleman that snaps your frame work to it. That's the clock your whole UI runs on, and it's the entire subject of Episode 10, so I'll keep it to one sentence here: you don't render when you decide to; you render when vsync says go, and the gap between two vsyncs is your budget.The important consequence for this episode is that the budget is not a constant your code carries around. It's a property of the display, read at runtime. And the framework already knows it, which is why the famous "Skipped frames!" warning is computed against the real interval, not against 16ms.What does "Skipped N frames!" actually measure?Everyone has seen this in Logcat:I/Choreographer: Skipped 47 frames! The application may be doing too much work on its main thread.Most developers read it as a vague scold. It's not vague at all. It's a precise division, and reading the source tells you two things the message hides. Here's doFrame in Choreographer.java:Press enter or click to view image in full sizeChoreographer.doFrame on cs.android.com. jitterNanos is how late this frame is versus its intended vsync; frameIntervalNanos is the real per-frame interval derived from the display's refresh rate. The warning only fires when skippedFrames >= SKIPPED_FRAME_WARNING_LIMIT.// frameworks/base/core/java/android/view/Choreographer.javafinal long skippedFrames = jitterNanos / frameIntervalNanos;if (skippedFrames >= SKIPPED_FRAME_WARNING_LIMIT) { Log.i(TAG, "Skipped " + skippedFrames + " frames! " + "The application may be doing too much work on its main " + "thread.");}First: skippedFrames is jitterNanos / frameIntervalNanos. frameIntervalNanos is the actual interval for the current display: at 120Hz it's about 8.3 million nanos, not 16. The system divides by the real budget. It always knew the number you've been ignoring.Second, and this is the trap: SKIPPED_FRAME_WARNING_LIMIT defaults to 30.private static final int SKIPPED_FRAME_WARNING_LIMIT = SystemProperties.getInt( "debug.choreographer.skipwarning", 30);Thirty skipped frames. At 60Hz that's half a second of frozen UI before Logcat says one word. At 120Hz it's a quarter second. The absence of "Skipped frames!" does not mean your app is smooth. It means you haven't stalled for 30 consecutive frames. Single dropped frames, the ones that read as visible hitching during a scroll, never trip this log at all. If you've been using its silence as a green light, you've been grading yourself on a test that only fails catastrophic freezes.So what moves the budget at runtime?Variable refresh rate. On modern panels the refresh rate isn't even fixed for the life of your app. The system raises and lowers it to match content and save power, which means the budget target slides out from under you while you run.Android 15 formalized this as Adaptive Refresh Rate (ARR): with the right HAL support, the display continuously adapts its refresh rate to the content's frame rate using discrete VSync steps, rather than being pinned to one mode. You feed the system your intent with the frame rate API, Surface.setFrameRate(...), available since Android 11 (API 30), and it picks a refresh rate to match. A video scene might run the panel at 60Hz; a flung list might push it to 120Hz; an idle screen might drop to 1Hz to save battery.Press enter or click to view image in full sizeVRR/ARR in one picture: as the panel shifts refresh rate to match content and save power, the per-frame budget shifts with it. A target you optimized against once is not the target you’re rendering against now.So the question "what's my frame budget?" has no single ans

Play Store Rejects Your AppIf you’re a Flutter developer, you may have recently received a warning from the Google Play Console asking you to:Upgrade image_picker_androidUpgrade everything you need.Why Google Play Is Asking You to ChangeGoogle has tightened its Photo and Video Permissions policy.Apps that only allow users to select photos or videos occasionally should not request broad access to the device’s media library.Instead, they should use the Android Photo Picker, which provides secure access to user-selected files without requiring storage permissions.This Good NewsIf you’re already using Flutter’s image_picker, your Dart code probably doesn't need to change.Most of the work involves:Updating packagesRemoving unnecessary permissionsStep 1: Update Your PackagesUpgrade to the latest image_picker.dependencies: image_picker: ^1.2.0If Google specifically asks for newer Android implementations, you can temporarily use:dependency_overrides: android:name="android.permission.READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE" tools:node="remove"/></manifest>Step 3: Remove Runtime Permission RequestsMany apps still do this:await Permission.photos.request();await Permission.storage.request();await Permission.videos.request();These are no longer needed for normal image selection with image_picker.Simply remove them.Step 4: Keep Using ImagePicker NormallyYour existing code can remain exactly the same.final picker = ImagePicker();final image = await picker.pickImage( source: ImageSource.gallery,);final video = await picker.pickVideo( source: ImageSource.gallery,);On supported Android versions, Flutter automatically uses the Android Photo Picker behind the scenes.No storage permission dialog appears.Step 5: Verify Your Release BuildAfter building your app:flutter build appbundleCheck the generated bundle.If you still seeREAD_MEDIA_IMAGESREAD_MEDIA_VIDEOREAD_EXTERNAL_STORAGEthen another dependency is adding them.You can inspect the merged manifest with:./gradlew app:processReleaseMainManifestCommon MistakesUsing permission_handler unnecessarilyIf you’re only selecting images from the gallery, don’t request storage permissions.Old image_picker versionsOlder versions don’t fully support Android Photo Picker.Always update to the latest stable release.A dependency reintroduces permissionsSome camera, file picker, access, such as:Gallery appsPhoto editorsBackup applicationsFile managersMedia management toolsIn those cases, you may still request the necessary permissions, but you’ll need to justify them in the Google Play Console and comply with Google’s Photo and Video Permissions policy.Benefits of MigratingNo storage permission dialogBetter user privacyEasier Play Store approvalCleaner AndroidManifestLess permission-related codeFuture-proof for upcoming Android versionsFinal ThoughtsGoogle is clearly moving Android toward user-selected media access instead of full storage access. The Android Photo Picker is now the recommended approach for most Flutter apps.For most developers, the migration is surprisingly simple:Update image_pickerRemove storage permissionsStop requesting runtime storage permissionsPublish with confidenceA few minutes of work today can save you from Play Console warnings — or even app update rejections — in the future.ReferencesGoogle Play — Photo and Video Permissions Policy: https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/15800983Android Developers — Photo Picker: https://developer.android.com/training/data-storage/shared/photopickerFlutter image_picker package: https://pub.dev/packages/image_picker

content: AndroidMobile App DevelopmentMvvmJetpack ComposeMVVM vs MVI in Android: XML Views and Jetpack Compose, Side by SideMuhammad Awais5 min read·6 days ago--ListenShareBy Awais — Android developer, devawais.comPress enter or click to view image in full sizeThis image was generated using chatgptI already wrote about when to pick MVVM vs MVI — that’s a separate piece if you want the decision framework without wading through code. This one’s the opposite: no philosophy, just what these two patterns actually look like when you build the same screen four ways — MVVM with XML, MVI with XML, MVVM with Compose, MVI with Compose.I used the same test case for all four: a “search and filter a list of products” screen, backed by the same repository, same Clean Architecture use case underneath. Only the presentation layer changes. If you want to run them yourself — the snippets here are trimmed for readability.The setupdata class Product(val id: String, val name: String, val price: Double)interface ProductRepository { suspend fun search(query: String): List<Product>}That’s it, that’s the whole domain contract. Everything below is just presentation.MVVM — XML / View systemThe ViewModel exposes several independent StateFlows:class ProductViewModel( private val repository: ProductRepository) : ViewModel() {private val _products = MutableStateFlow<List<Product>>(emptyList()) val products: StateFlow<List<Product>> = _products private val _isLoading = MutableStateFlow(false) val isLoading: StateFlow<Boolean> = _isLoading private val _error = MutableStateFlow<String?>(null) val error: StateFlow<String?> = _error private val _searchQuery = MutableStateFlow("") val searchQuery: StateFlow<String> = _searchQuery fun onSearchQueryChanged(query: String) { _searchQuery.value = query fetchProducts(query) } private fun fetchProducts(query: String) { viewModelScope.launch { _isLoading.value = true try { _products.value = repository.search(query) _error.value = null } catch (e: Exception) { _error.value = e.message } finally { _isLoading.value = false } } }}And the Fragment ends up combining those streams manually, because a derived condition like “show empty state” depends on all three at once:viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch { combine(viewModel.products, viewModel.isLoading, viewModel.error) { products, loading, error -> Triple(products, loading, error) }.collect { (products, loading, error) -> emptyStateView.isVisible = products.isEmpty() && !loading && error == null loadingView.isVisible = loading errorView.isVisible = error != null recyclerAdapter.submitList(products) }}searchBar.doOnTextChanged { text, _, _, _ -> viewModel.onSearchQueryChanged(text.toString())}Works fine. But that combine {} block is doing real work the ViewModel could've done for it — and it's the kind of code that gets copy-pasted into every screen that needs a derived UI state.MVI — XML / View systemSame repository, one State object instead of four flows:data class ProductScreenState( val products: List<Product> = emptyList(), val isLoading: Boolean = false, val error: String? = null, val searchQuery: String = "") { val isEmptyStateVisible: Boolean get() = products.isEmpty() && !isLoading && error == null}sealed interface ProductIntent { data class SearchQueryChanged(val query: String) : ProductIntent object Retry : ProductIntent}class ProductViewModel( private val repository: ProductRepository) : ViewModel() { private val _state = MutableStateFlow(ProductScreenState()) val state: StateFlow<ProductScreenState> = _state fun onIntent(intent: ProductIntent) { when (intent) { is ProductIntent.SearchQueryChanged -> search(intent.query) is ProductIntent.Retry -> search(_state.value.searchQuery) } } private fun search(query: String) { _state.update { it.copy(searchQuery = query, isLoading = true, error = null) } viewModelScope.launch { try { val results = repository.search(query) _state.update { it.copy(products = results, isLoading = false) } } catch (e: Exception) { _state.update { it.copy(isLoading = false, error = e.message) } } } }}The Fragment collapses to one collector, and isEmptyStateVisible is a derived property on the State itself — it can never disagree with the rest of the snapshot, because it's computed from the same object, not from streams racing each other:viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch { viewModel.state.collect { state -> emptyStateView.isVisible = state.isEmptyStateVisible loadingView.isVisible = state.isLoading errorView.isVisible = state.error != null recyclerAdapter.submitList(state.products) }}searchBar.doOnTextChanged { text, _, _, _ -> title: MVVM vs MVI in Android: A Practical Guide to Choosing the Right Architecture
excerpt: By Awais — Senior Mobile App Developer, devawais.com Continue reading on Medium »
content: Android ArchitectureMvvmClean ArchitectureAndroidMobile App DevelopmentMVVM vs MVI in Android: A Practical Guide to Choosing the Right ArchitectureMuhammad Awais6 min read·5 days ago--ListenShareBy Awais — Senior Mobile App Developer, devawais.comPress enter or click to view image in full sizeThis image was created using CHAT GPTI’m Awais, and I want to start with a confession — I used to think MVI was just MVVM with extra steps. I said that out loud in a code review once and got roasted for it, rightfully so. So I went and actually built the same feature — a fairly boring “search and filter a list of products” screen — in both patterns, back to back, over a weekend, just to settle the argument in my own head.This article is the “which one should I actually use” side of that experiment — no code walkthroughs here, I’ve got a separate implementation-focused piece for that (linked at the bottom, with full XML and Jetpack Compose examples side by side). This one’s for the decision itself: what each pattern is actually good at, where each one quietly falls apart, and how I now decide per-screen instead of picking a side once and defending it forever.If your team is arguing about this in Slack right now — mine did — hopefully this settles it faster than my weekend did.What these two patterns are actually solvingBoth MVVM and MVI exist to separate your UI from your logic. Neither one is “the architecture” for your app — they’re presentation-layer patterns, usually sitting on top of a Clean Architecture setup with use cases and repositories underneath. The real difference between them isn’t philosophical; it’s mechanical: how they handle state.MVVM — Model, View, ViewModel. The ViewModel exposes state, often as several independent LiveData or StateFlow fields (loading, data, error, and so on). The View observes each of them and calls functions on the ViewModel in response to user actions.MVI — Model, View, Intent. The View sends Intents — user actions represented as data — into the ViewModel, which acts as a reducer and produces one single, immutable State object. The View has exactly one thing to render.That “one state object vs several independent fields” distinction is the whole ballgame. Every pro and con below traces back to it.Where MVVM genuinely shinesI want to say this clearly, because a lot of MVI-evangelist content makes MVVM sound broken, and it isn’t:Lower learning curve. Almost every Android dev already half-knows this pattern from tutorials, docs, and general industry exposure.Less boilerplate for simple screens. A settings toggle or a static info screen doesn’t need a sealed Intent hierarchy — that’s just ceremony for something trivial.Deep tooling alignment. Data Binding, LiveData, and ViewModel scoping were largely designed with MVVM assumptions in mind, so things tend to “just work.”Faster to prototype. If you’re quickly validating a UI idea, MVVM gets you there with less setup.Where MVVM starts to hurtThe problem shows up the moment a screen needs a derived condition — say, an “empty state” that depends on loading, data, and error all being in a specific combination at once. You end up combining several independent streams manually in the View to answer “what should actually be on screen right now.”And that’s the real issue: nothing structurally stops your state fields from drifting out of sync with each other. You can genuinely end up with isLoading = true and non-empty data at the same moment, for a fraction of a frame, and now your UI is defensively guessing what's "really" happening instead of just rendering a fact.State fragmentation across multiple independent fields.Debugging is harder — there’s no single “here’s exactly what the screen looked like at 3:42:10pm” snapshot to inspect.Testing gets awkward past five or six interacting fields; you end up combining them manually in tests too.Encourages state-combination logic to leak into the View layer, which is exactly where you don’t want business-adjacent logic living.Where MVI genuinely shinesSingle source of truth. One state, one render function. This alone eliminates a whole category of “how did the UI get into this combination” bugs.Predictable and testable. Every state transition is a near-pure function of (currentState, intent), so you can unit test the reducer without touching a single Android framework class.Trivial state logging and time-travel debugging, since every emission is a complete snapshot you can just log and replay.Scales well on genuinely stateful screens — checkout flows, multi-step forms, anything with a lot of conditional UI.Fits naturally with Clean Architecture and unidirectional data flow, if your domain layer already returns sealed Result types from use cases — MVI just continues that same philosophy up into the presentation layer instead of breaking it.Where MVI starts to hurtMore boilerplate up front — a sealed Intent hierarchy, a State data class, often a separate Effect channel for one-off events.Genuinely overkill for simple screens. I wouldn’t reach for full MVI on a static “About” page.Real learning curve for teams new to unidirectional data flow — “why can’t I just update this one field” is a question I’ve answered more than once.Without discipline, you can still end up with a 300-line when block in the reducer — it's one big function instead of scattered fields, but it's still a mess if nobody's watching it.So how do I actually decide, per screenI stopped treating this as an ideological, project-wide choice a while ago. It’s a per-screen decision now, and here’s roughly the checklist I run through:Reach for MVVM when:The screen has one to three independent pieces of state that genuinely don’t interact much — a settings screen is the classic example.You’re prototyping, and speed matters more than long-term maintainability right now.Junior devs are still ramping up, and you want something they can be productive in immediately, without a unidirectional-data-flow crash course first.Reach

title: Reality : Anxiety Is Real And I Think We All Have It
excerpt: Do you know that strange dread that washes over you when you close TikTok and just sit there? That’s not boredom. That’s reality anxiety. Continue reading on Medium »
content: Mental HealthAISocial MediaAndroidPapercraft PublisherReality : Anxiety Is Real And I Think We All Have ItPapercraft Publishers3 min read·6 days ago--ListenShareDo you know that strange dread that washes over you when you close TikTok and just sit there? That’s not boredom. That’s reality anxiety.Almost every Gen Z I know experiences it.We grew up with a phone in our hand, an algorithm giving us a dopamine hit every eight seconds. We got accustomed to life being fast, loud, edited, and filtered. Now, real life feels slow, quiet, and unedited. Our brains struggle to handle this shift. The moment we’re not stimulated, we panic. We call it "being bored," but it’s really anxiety. Anxiety that nothing’s happening. Anxiety that we might be missing out. Anxiety that if we’re not scrolling, producing, or posting, we’re falling behind.Press enter or click to view image in full sizeThe issue is we never learned how to just exist. We learned to react. To a trend, to a meme, to other people’s lives. But sitting with your own thoughts, without music, a screen, or a plan? That feels wrong. It feels like wasting time. I caught myself feeling guilty for taking a 20-minute walk without a podcast. It seemed like I should’ve been "using that time" for something. That’s crazy.Reality anxiety shows up in small ways. Checking your phone mid-conversation. Needing background noise to fall asleep. Feeling restless on weekends. Thinking you must turn everything into content or it didn’t count. We’re so afraid of missing out that we miss living our own lives.I don’t think the solution is deleting everything and moving to the mountains. But I do believe we need to retrain our brains to be okay with being bored. Boredom is where ideas are born. Calm is where healing happens. Silence is where you truly hear yourself.So, I’m trying this: 10 minutes a day with no phone. No music. No goal. Just me and my thoughts. The first week was torture. Now it’s the only time I feel like myself again.Press enter or click to view image in full sizeIf you’ve ever felt anxious for no reason after putting your phone down, that’s it. That’s reality anxiety. And you’re not broken. You’re just overstimulated.Let’s start getting comfortable with real life again. One boring, quiet, unproductive minute at a time.

title: How I Built a Flipkart-Style Order Tracking Timeline in Flutter
excerpt: When we shop online, one of the first things we check after placing an order is where our package has reached. Continue reading on Medium »
content: FlutterAndroidIOSOrder TrackingDartHow I Built a Flipkart-Style Order Tracking Timeline in FlutterAnkit Mehra4 min read·6 days ago--ListenSharePress enter or click to view image in full sizeWhen we shop online, one of the first things we check after placing an order is where our package has reached. Whether it’s a phone, a pair of shoes, or groceries, tracking the delivery has become a normal part of the shopping experience.Apps like Flipkart make this experience simple by displaying every stage of an order in a clean vertical timeline. Instead of showing only the current status, they let us see the complete journey — from order placement to delivery — along with timestamps for each update.Recently, I wanted to add a similar tracking experience to one of our Flutter applications. Rather than building the entire timeline from scratch, I explored an approach that provides a smooth animated order tracker while still allowing customization of the tracking information.In this article, i will explain that how i implemented a Flipkart-style order tracking timeline in Flutter and how easily it can be integrated into any e-commerce, food delivery, pharmacy, or logistics application.Why we should add an Order Tracking Timeline?An order tracking screen is much more than a progress indicator.It helps users:(i). Understand the current delivery stage.(ii). See every completed milestone.(iii). Reduce uncertainty after placing an order.(iv). Improve trust in the application.(v). Get a familiar shopping experience similar to popular e-commerce apps.Even if your application isn’t an online shopping platform, this type of timeline works well for:(i). Food delivery(ii). Medicine delivery(iii). Courier services(iv). Laundry applications(v). Parcel tracking(vi). Service booking appsAdding the DependencyWe have to add the order_tracker package in our pubspec.yaml file.dependencies: order_tracker: ^0.0.2Then we have to run this command for install this package.flutter pub getPreparing the Tracking DataEach stage contains a title and an optional date.List<TextDto> orderList = [ TextDto( "Your order has been placed", "Fri, 25th Mar '22 - 10:47pm", ), TextDto( "Seller has processed your order", "Sun, 27th Mar '22 - 10:19am", ), TextDto( "Courier partner picked up your order", "Tue, 29th Mar '22 - 5:00pm", ),];The same structure can be used for every delivery stage.List<TextDto> shippedList = [ TextDto( "Your order has been shipped", "Tue, 29th Mar '22 - 5:04pm", ), TextDto( "Package reached the nearest hub", null, ),];List<TextDto> outForDeliveryList = [ TextDto( "Your order is out for delivery", "Thu, 31st Mar '22 - 2:27pm", ),];List<TextDto> deliveredList = [ TextDto( "Your order has been delivered", "Thu, 31st Mar '22 - 3:58pm", ),];Keeping every milestone in a separate list makes the tracking information much easier to organize and update.Building the TimelineOnce the data is ready, displaying the tracker only requires a single widget.OrderTracker( status: Status.delivered, activeColor: Colors.green, inActiveColor: Colors.grey[300], orderTitleAndDateList: orderList, shippedTitleAndDateList: shippedList, outOfDeliveryTitleAndDateList: outForDeliveryList, deliveredTitleAndDateList: deliveredList,)The widget automatically displays the completed steps and highlights the current delivery status.Understanding the StatusThe status property controls which step is currently active.For example:Status.ordershows that the order has just been placed.Status.shippedupdates the UI until the shipping stage.Status.outOfDeliverymarks the package as out for delivery.Status.deliveredcompletes the entire tracking timeline.Changing a single value is enough to update the complete progress indicator.Customizing the AppearanceThe timeline can easily match your application’s branding.activeColor: Colors.green,inActiveColor: Colors.grey.shade300,The active color highlights completed milestones, while inactive sections remain subtle until they are completed.This small customization helps maintain visual consistency with the rest of the application.Where this UI can be usedAlthough this design is commonly seen in shopping applications, it works well in many other scenarios.(i). Online shopping(ii). Grocery delivery(iii). Food delivery(iv). Medicine delivery(v). Courier tracking(vi). Laundry services(vii). Home service booking(viii). Document delivery(ix). Repair service trackingAny workflow that moves through multiple stages can benefit from this timeline layout.Things to keep in mindBefore integrating this into a production application, consider a few improvements.(i). Fetch tracking data from an API instead of hardcoding it.(ii). Update the timeline in real time whenever the order status changes.(iii). Localize timestamps for different regions.(iv). Display estimated delivery dates.(v). Show courier information and tracking IDs.(vi). Handle cancelled or returned orders.(vii). Better anime selection than most people expect, weighted toward completed series.- Funimation — Merging into Crunchyroll but still operational.
