content: AndroidAndroid DevelopmentKotlinJetpack ComposeCodingANDROID INTERNALS · PREDICTIVE BACKAndroid’s predictive back gesture, explained from zeroLuca Fioravanti15 min read·Just now--ListenSharePress enter or click to view image in full sizeSwipe back on a recent Android phone and the screen you’re leaving doesn’t just vanish. It shrinks and slides toward the edge while the screen underneath it slides into view, live, following your finger. Lift before you’re happy with what you see and it snaps back like nothing happened. That live preview is Android’s predictive back gesture, and this article explains what it is, how to wire it up on the three surfaces you’ll actually build with (plain Views, Fragments, Compose), and then goes deeper into three things about it that are easy to get wrong even once you know the basics.If you’ve never touched this API before, start with the next section. If you already know what onBackStarted/onBackProgressed mean and just want the three gotchas, skip to "The one dispatcher everything else in this article shares."What “back” used to mean, and what changedBefore Android 13, pressing back (a physical button, an on-screen button, or a swipe gesture, depending on the device) did one thing: it popped whatever was on top, instantly. The system didn’t show you where you were headed. You pressed back, and the current screen was simply replaced by whatever was underneath it, or the app closed, or you landed on the home screen. If you weren’t sure what “back” would do, the only way to find out was to do it and see.That instant swap is also why back gestures used to feel risky. Swipe from the edge, and either you get taken exactly where you expected, or you don’t, and by the time you know which, you’ve already left the screen you were on. There was no preview and no way to bail out mid-gesture.Predictive back changes the mechanics, not the destination. When you start a back swipe now, the system treats it as a question rather than a command: it shows you a live, interactive preview of where “back” would take you, scrubbing in sync with your finger, and only actually commits to leaving the current screen once you lift your finger past a commit point. Drag less than that, or reverse direction, and the preview reverses too. You get to see the answer before you agree to it.Under the hood, every back gesture on a predictive-back-aware app goes through the same four moments, and it’s worth understanding these in plain language before you see a single API name:The gesture starts. Your finger touches down near the edge and begins to move. The system tells the app “a back gesture has begun,” so the app can get ready: stop whatever animation might already be running, prepare the screen it would be going back to.The gesture progresses. As long as your finger keeps moving, the system keeps telling the app how far along the swipe is, as a fraction from just-started to fully-committed. The app uses that fraction to drive whatever it’s showing you: how far the card has slid, how much the destination screen has faded in, and so on. This repeats many times a second while your finger is moving, which is what makes the animation feel like it’s tracking your thumb instead of just playing on a timer.You commit. Lift your finger past the threshold, and the system tells the app the gesture is done: finish the animation, and actually perform whatever “back” means here (close a screen, pop a fragment, navigate to a previous destination).You cancel. Lift before the threshold, or drag back toward where you started, and the system tells the app the gesture was abandoned: animate back to where things were, and don’t navigate anywhere.Everything else in this article is those four moments, started / progressed / committed / cancelled, wearing different API names depending on which part of Android you're writing code against. Once that mental model is in place, the actual method names (onBackStarted, onBackProgressed, onBackInvoked, onBackCancelled, and their AndroidX equivalents you'll see below) are just labels on a shape you already understand.One more piece of vocabulary worth having up front: progress. It's a number from just above 0 (gesture just started) to 1 (fully committed), and every surface below hands it to you as a plain Float. If you remember nothing else from this section, remember that progress is "how far the user has dragged," and every animation in this article is some UI property set as a function of that one number.The basic shape of the API on each surfaceBefore any of the interesting edge cases, here’s the minimum code you’d actually type to hook into a back gesture on each of the three surfaces this article covers. None of these use the progress/preview behavior yet, they just react when the gesture commits, which is enough for the vast majority of real back-handling code (closing a screen, popping a stack, showing a confirmation dialog).Views and Activities. Every ComponentActivity already exposes an onBackPressedDispatcher. Registering a callback against it looks like this:class MainActivity : ComponentActivity() { override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) { super.onCreate(savedInstanceState) setContentView(R.layout.activity_main) onBackPressedDispatcher.addCallback(this) { // Runs when the user presses/swipes back and the gesture commits. finish() } }}addCallback(owner, onBackPressed) is a small Kotlin convenience: pass a LifecycleOwner (here, the activity itself) and a lambda for the commit case, and it builds an enabled OnBackPressedCallback for you behind the scenes. The day I saw that video, I made a decision: I am not going to do Web Development.When I entered college, club recruitments for first-year students were going on, and with no technical knowledge, I had no idea what I should do. I filled out three club recruitment forms. In one of them, I chose Cybersecurity as the domain because I thought it would be cool, but sadly, I was rejected.For the other two clubs, I applied for App Development. Luckily, I got selected in both. The funny part was that I wasn’t even aware of terms like Flutter, XML, or Kotlin at that time. In one club, I was assigned App Development with Kotlin, while in the other, I was assigned App Development with Flutter.But as human nature says, don’t do it alone. So, I told my friend about it. He was also selected for the club where I was assigned Kotlin. Originally, he was going for Web Development because he thought JavaScript and Java were the same thing. Keep navigation execution native. AppRoute.showDetail( showId: showId ))🏗️ Architecture DecisionThe shared layer owns the meaning:ShowDetail(showId)Each platform maps that intent to its native route type.Shared Destination ↓ShowDetail(showId) ↙ ↘Android Route iOS RouteThis gives us type safety without forcing Android and iOS to share the same navigation framework.✅ Quick RecapAvoid raw route strings.Share semantic title: Day — 17: How Instagram Builds the Feed That Keeps You Scrolling [System Design]
excerpt: Every time you open Instagram, a system decides in milliseconds which posts you see, in what order, from millions of options. Continue reading on Medium »
content: Press enter or click to view image in full sizeDesign SystemsMobileAndroidAndroid DevelopmentAndroid App DevelopmentDay — 17: How Instagram Builds the Feed That Keeps You Scrolling [System Design]Every time you open Instagram, a system decides in milliseconds which posts you see, in what order, from millions of options. Here’s how it works.Ahmed Kenawy5 min read·Just now--ListenShareThe ProblemYou follow 500 people on Instagram. Each posts 3 times a day. That’s 1,500 potential posts every single day — just for you.When you open the app, it needs to show you the most relevant ones, in the right order, in under 100 milliseconds.How does it decide? How does it fetch them fast enough? And how do you build something similar?Think of It Like a NewspaperA regular newspaper prints the same thing for everyone. Slow to make, same for all readers.A personalized newspaper would be printed fresh for you every morning — only the stories from the writers you follow, sorted by what you care about most.Your Instagram feed is that personalized newspaper. But printed in 100 milliseconds, for 2 billion people.The Two Core ApproachesThere are two ways to build a feed system. The choice defines your entire architecture.Approach 1 — Fan-out on Write (Push)When Ahmed posts a photo, the system immediately copies that post into the feed of every one of his followers. When you open the app — your feed is already ready. Just read it.Ahmed posts a photo ↓System finds all 1,000 of Ahmed's followers ↓Copies the post into each follower's feed table ↓You open the app → your feed is pre-built → instantFast to read. Expensive to write (especially for celebrities with 50M followers).Approach 2 — Fan-out on Read (Pull)When you open your feed, the system finds everyone you follow, fetches their recent posts, merges them, sorts them, and shows you the result.You open the app ↓System finds all 500 people you follow ↓Fetches recent posts from each ↓Merges + sorts everything ↓Shows you the resultCheap to write. Slow to read (the more people you follow, the slower it gets).What Instagram actually does: Both. Regular users → Fan-out on write (pre-built feed) Celebrities with 50M+ followers → Fan-out on read (too expensive to copy to 50M feeds)Press enter or click to view image in full sizeFeed Pagination — Never Load Everything at OnceYou don’t load all 1,500 posts at once. You load 20, then 20 more when the user scrolls down. This is called pagination.The right way to paginate a feed is with a cursor — not a page number.❌ Page-based pagination (wrong)GET /feed?page=2Problem: if a new post is added between page 1 and page 2,you either see the same post twice or skip one entirely.✅ Cursor-based pagination (right)GET /feed?cursor=post_id_of_last_item_seenThe cursor is the ID of the last post you saw."Give me posts that come after this one."New posts don't break your position.Press enter or click to view image in full sizeAndroid Implementation// Feed data modeldata class FeedPost( val id : String, val authorId : String, val authorName : String, val authorAvatar: String, val imageUrl : String, val caption : String, val likeCount : Int, val createdAt : Long)data class FeedResponse( val posts : List<FeedPost>, val nextCursor : String?, // null = no more posts val hasMore : Boolean)// API - cursor-based paginationinterface FeedApi { @GET("v1/feed") suspend fun getFeed( @Query("cursor") cursor: String? = null, // null = first page @Query("limit") limit : Int = 20 ): FeedResponse}// ViewModel - infinite scroll with cursorclass FeedViewModel @Inject constructor( private val api : FeedApi, private val dao : FeedDao) : ViewModel() { private val _posts = MutableStateFlow<List<FeedPost>>(emptyList()) val posts: StateFlow<List<FeedPost>> = _posts private val _isLoading = MutableStateFlow(false) val isLoading: StateFlow<Boolean> = _isLoading private var cursor : String? = null // tracks our position in the feed private var hasMore: Boolean = true init { loadFeed() } fun loadFeed() { if (_isLoading.value || !hasMore) return viewModelScope.launch { _isLoading.value = true try { val response = api.getFeed(cursor = cursor, limit = 20) // Append new posts to the existing list _posts.update { current -> current + response.posts } // Save cursor for next page cursor = response.nextCursor hasMore = response.hasMore // Cache first page locally for offline viewing if (cursor == null) dao.replaceAll(response.posts) } catch (e: IOException) { // No internet - show cached posts if (_posts.value.isEmpty()) { _posts.value = dao.getAll() } } finally { _isLoading.value = false } } } // Called when user scrolls near the bottom fun onScrolledToBottom() = loadFeed() // Pull-to-refresh - reset everything fun refresh() { cursor = null hasMore = true _posts.value = emptyList() loadFeed() }}// LazyColumn with infinite scroll trigger@Composablefun FeedScreen(viewModel: FeedViewModel = hiltViewModel()) { val posts by viewModel.posts.collectAsState() val isLoading by viewModel.isLoading.collectAsState() val listState = rememberLazyListState() LazyColumn(state = listState) { items(posts, key = { it.id }) { post -> FeedPostItem(post = post) } if (isLoading) { item { LoadingSpinner() } } } // Trigger next page when user is near bottom LaunchedEffect(listState) { snapshotFlow { listState.layoutInfo } .collect { info -> val lastVisible = info.visibleItemsInfo.lastOrNull()?.index ?: 0 val total = info.totalItemsCount if (lastVisible >= total - 5) { // 5 items from the end viewModel.onScrolledToBottom() } } }}Common MistakesMistake 1 — Loading all posts at once// ❌ Returns thousands of posts — slow, expensive, crashes on small phones@GET("v1/feed") suspend fun getFeed(): List<FeedPost>// ✅ Always paginate - 20 at a time, cursor-based@GET("v1/feed") suspend fun getFeed(@Query("cursor") cursor: String?, @Query("limit") limit: Int = 20): FeedResponseMistake 2 — Page-number pagination// ❌ Page numbers break when new posts arriveGET /feed?page=2 // user sees duplicates or skips posts

title: Put Compose State Where the Decision Lives
excerpt: A practical way to stop every piece of UI state from drifting into a ViewModel Continue reading on Medium »
content: AndroidSenior Software EngineerSoftware DevelopmentMobile AppKotlin ComposePut Compose State Where the Decision LivesGourango Sutradhar (Gourab)4 min read·Just now--ListenShareA practical way to stop every piece of UI state from drifting into a ViewModelA Compose screen can look tidy while its state model quietly becomes difficult to change. The usual warning sign is a ViewModel that owns everything: loading data, a selected tab, an expanded card, list position, a half-written search query, and perhaps a dialog flag for good measure.That setup is easy to start. It is much harder to explain six months later.The better question is not “Should this go in a ViewModel?” Ask: Who needs to read it, who can change it, and how long must it survive?Start with the smallest honest ownerAndroid’s Compose guidance says state should stay close to where it is consumed and be hoisted to the lowest common ancestor of every composable that reads or writes it.[2]That rule is useful because it resists two common mistakes. Keeping state too low creates duplicate sources of truth. Hoisting it too high exposes details to parts of the screen that have no business knowing about them.A disclosure row is a simple example:@Composablefun DetailsRow(label: String) {var expanded by rememberSaveable { mutableStateOf(false) }Column {Text(text = label,modifier = Modifier.clickable { expanded = !expanded })if (expanded) {DetailsContent()}}}If no sibling needs expanded, leaving it inside DetailsRow is reasonable. The official hoisting guide makes the same point for simple UI element state: keeping it internal is acceptable when the logic is local and other parts of the hierarchy do not need control.[2]Moving this flag into a screen ViewModel would add an event, a field, and a dependency without solving a real problem.Hoist when another reader appearsSuppose a “Collapse all” action now needs to control several rows. The ownership boundary has changed. The state belongs at the nearest parent shared by the rows and that action.A stateless row becomes useful here:@Composablefun DetailsRow(label: String,expanded: Boolean,onExpandedChange: (Boolean) -> Unit) {Column {Text(text = label,modifier = Modifier.clickable {onExpandedChange(!expanded)})if (expanded) DetailsContent()}}This follows Compose’s usual state-hoisting shape: pass the current value down and send an event up. Hoisted state gives the caller control while the child stays reusable and easier to test.[1]Do not hoist by reflex, though. A longer parameter list is not automatically bad. Explicit parameters show what a composable reads and what it can request. Android’s guidance even prefers visible event parameters over wrapper objects that hide a composable’s responsibilities.[2]Separate UI logic from business logicThe hardest state decisions usually become easier once the logic is named.A scroll position, animation progress, or expanded row is UI element state. A repository-backed list, checkout eligibility, or a set of search results belongs to screen state shaped by business rules.The Compose guide recommends a ViewModel for screen state that needs business logic or access to data layers. It also warns against passing the ViewModel down through child composables; the screen-level composable can collect state and pass only the required values and events.[2]A useful boundary looks like this:@Composablefun SearchRoute(viewModel: SearchViewModel = viewModel()) {val uiState by viewModel.uiState.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()SearchScreen(uiState = uiState,onQueryChange = viewModel::updateQuery,onRetry = viewModel::retry)}SearchScreen does not know where results came from. Preview code can supply a plain SearchUiState, and tests can call it without constructing the screen’s data dependencies.For Android apps, the Compose state guide recommends collectAsStateWithLifecycle() when collecting a Flow into Compose state because collection follows the Android lifecycle.[1]Choose survival deliberatelyState location and state survival are related, but they are not the same decision.remember retains a value across recomposition, then forgets it when that composable leaves the composition. rememberSaveable can also restore values after activity recreation or system-initiated process recreation when the value can be saved.[1]That does not mean every local flag needs rememberSaveable. Ask whether restoring it helps the user.A half-written form field probably should survive rotation. A temporary pressed state should not. Restoring a transient animation at an arbitrary frame may be stranger than starting it again.For ViewModel-owned state, save only the minimum information needed to rebuild the screen. A search query or selected item ID is a better saved value than a large rendered UI model copied from the repository.A review checklist that catches most mistakesBefore approving a Compose screen, trace each mutable value and ask:Which composables read it?2. Which actions can change it?3. Is the logic purely visual, or does it apply a product rule?4. Must it survive recomposition, activity recreation, or process recreation?5. Can the child receive a value and event instead of a ViewModel?6. Is there one source of truth, or did convenience create a second copy?The answers usually point to one of four owners: the composable itself, a shared parent, a plain state holder for complex UI logic, or a screen-level ViewModel for business logic.A clean state model is less about picking the fanciest abstraction and more about keeping each decision close to the code that can honestly make it.Sources[1] State and Jetpack Compose | Android Developershttps://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/state[2] Where to hoist state | Jetpack Compose | Android Developershttps://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/state-hoisting

title: What I Found While Investigating Samsung’s Hidden Galaxy AI Settings
excerpt: The Starting Point Continue reading on Medium »
content: AndroidSamsungGalaxyaiSamsung Galaxy AiSamsung GalaxyWhat I Found While Investigating Samsung’s Hidden Galaxy AI SettingsPrashant Kumar4 min read·1 hour ago--ListenShareThe Starting PointI came across a Samsung Settings activity related to Galaxy AI / Intelligence Service and tried launching it through Activity Launcher.Instead of opening the expected settings page, it immediately returned to the previous screen.My first assumption was that the activity might be crashing.Rather than stopping there, I decided to investigate what Android and Samsung’s framework were actually doing.Starting the Investigation with ADBI first identified the activity through Samsung’s Settings package and confirmed that it was a legitimate exported activity.I then launched it directly through ADB using Samsung’s registered intent.The result was interesting: Android reported that the activity launched successfully.There was no indication that the activity itself was invalid.That shifted the investigation from:“Why is Android unable to launch this activity?”to:“What happens after the activity launches?”Looking at LogcatThe next step was checking the system logs while launching the activity.There was no typical Android crash information such as a FATAL EXCEPTION.Instead, Samsung’s Settings application reported that the Intelligence Service was not supported.The activity was then closed.This was the first major discovery:The activity wasn’t crashing. Samsung’s own code was deciding that the feature wasn’t supported and closing the screen.Going Inside Samsung SettingsTo understand why Samsung considered the feature unsupported, I pulled the system Settings APK from the device.I then opened the APK with JADX and searched through Samsung’s decompiled source.The log message led directly to the IntelligenceServiceSettings implementation.There I found the logic responsible for deciding whether the Intelligence Service should be available.The settings screen checks a Samsung feature-support function.If that function reports that the Intelligence Service isn’t supported, the screen simply terminates.This gave me a clear direction for the investigation.Following the Feature-Support LogicI continued tracing the support function through Samsung’s code.The function ultimately depends on a Samsung feature flag called:FEATURE_INTELLIGENCE_SERVICEIf that feature flag is disabled, Samsung considers the Intelligence Service unsupported.At this point, the question became much more interesting:Who controls that feature flag?Finding Samsung’s Firmware-Level ConfigurationI traced the feature flag into Samsung’s Rune configuration system.The flag wasn’t simply hardcoded as enabled or disabled.Instead, Samsung derives it from a Samsung Floating Feature configuration.The specific configuration involved a setting named:SEC_FLOATING_FEATURE_COMMON_DISABLE_NATIVE_AII then searched the device’s Samsung floating-feature configuration.The value was explicitly set to:TRUEThat finally explained the entire behavior.Samsung’s Settings application sees that Native AI is disabled, translates that into the Intelligence Service being unsupported, and closes the activity.An Important DiscoveryAt first, it would be easy to conclude that the device simply doesn’t support Galaxy AI.However, the firmware configuration told a more complicated story.The same configuration contains multiple other AI-related capabilities, including support for AI agents, generative AI functionality, and other Samsung AI systems.So the situation isn’t:AI is completely unavailable.It’s closer to:Samsung has selectively disabled the Native AI / Intelligence Service functionality on this firmware.That distinction was the most interesting part of the investigation.Checking the Device ConfigurationI also checked the device’s model, firmware, and CSC information.The device was running Samsung firmware for the SM-E566B with the INS (India) CSC.I searched the relevant CSC and OMC configuration locations but found no separate configuration overriding the Native AI restriction.I also checked the installed Samsung AI-related packages.The relevant components were present, which further supported the conclusion that this wasn’t simply a missing-package problem.Why Couldn’t ADB Fix It?The next question was whether the feature could simply be enabled through ADB.I checked the device’s boot and security state.The device reported a locked bootloader and green verified-boot state.The Samsung floating-feature configuration is also located inside the protected system partition and is owned by root.Normal ADB shell access therefore isn’t sufficient to modify the configuration.This means that launching the hidden activity, enabling individual Samsung services, or installing related packages doesn’t change the underlying restriction.The decision is being made much earlier by Samsung’s firmware configuration.The Investigation in One SentenceWhat initially looked like a broken or crashing Galaxy AI settings activity turned out to be a deliberate Samsung feature restriction controlled by a firmware-level floating-feature flag.What I LearnedThis investigation reinforced an important lesson about Android internals:Seeing an activity doesn’t mean the feature behind it is enabled.An activity can exist in the APK, be registered in the manifest, have a valid intent, launch successfully, and still immediately close because an internal feature flag determines that the functionality isn’t supported.The investigation therefore moved through several layers:Activity Launcher → ADB → Logcat → Samsung Settings APK → JADX → Samsung framework code → Feature flag → Floating Feature configuration → Firmware restrictionWhat started as a simple attempt to open a hidden settings page became a practical look into how Samsung controls feature availability at the firmware level.
